title: Common Take-Home & Pairing Pitfalls
summary: The failure modes specific to unsupervised or collaborative formats — scope creep, ignored time budgets, and unclarified ambiguity — distinct from live solo-coding pitfalls.

slides.markdown:
The earlier topics in this group each covered one skill in isolation — [take-home-strategy](take-home-strategy), [take-home-submission-structure](take-home-submission-structure), and [pair-programming-format](pair-programming-format). This topic closes the group by naming the failure modes that recur across both unsupervised formats, distinct from the pitfalls of a live solo-coding round covered elsewhere.

What unites take-homes and pairing rounds is the **absence of constant supervision** — no one stopping you the moment you go off track. That absence is exactly what turns small misjudgments into large ones: scope creep goes unchecked for hours instead of minutes, an unclarified assumption compounds silently, and a skipped test only surfaces as a problem at review time.

slides.sectionTitle: Scope creep: building features nobody asked for
slides.markdown:
Scope creep on a take-home rarely looks like a deliberate decision — it looks like one small addition leading naturally to the next. You add a config option "while you're in there," which needs validation, which needs a test, which needs documentation, and three hours later you've built a subsystem the prompt never mentioned.

The defense is a concrete scope boundary written down **before** you start: list exactly what the prompt asks for, and treat anything outside that list as a candidate for the trade-offs section, not the code. If you find yourself adding something and can't point to which requirement it serves, that's the signal to stop and write it down as a deferred item instead.

Scope creep is costly specifically because it's invisible while it's happening — you feel productive the entire time, right up until you check the clock.

slides.sectionTitle: Ignoring the stated time budget entirely
slides.markdown:
A stated time budget ("this should take about 4 hours") is information about the intended scope, not a soft suggestion you can override with enough enthusiasm. Blowing well past it — a 4-hour prompt turning into 15 hours — doesn't read as extra effort; it reads as a candidate who can't calibrate scope to a constraint, which is precisely what the budget exists to test.

The common trap is treating "I have more time available this weekend" as a reason to use it, rather than checking whether the problem actually needs it. If you genuinely believe more time is warranted because the prompt is unusually large, say so explicitly rather than silently spending it — a note like "I estimate this needs 6-7 hours, not the suggested 4, because X" is honest calibration; silent overrun is not.

If you do go over, disclose the actual time spent. Evaluators calibrate their read against the number you report — an undisclosed 15-hour effort presented as if it took 4 misrepresents your actual working speed.

slides.sectionTitle: Not clarifying ambiguous requirements when working async
slides.markdown:
In a live round, an ambiguous requirement gets resolved in seconds by asking. In an async take-home, the same ambiguity has no immediate answer available, which pushes some candidates toward silently guessing rather than reaching out — and a wrong guess compounds for hours before anyone catches it.

The fix isn't to avoid ambiguity — most real prompts have some — it's to **triage it early**. If an ambiguity is genuinely architecture-changing, send one specific, well-framed question before building on an assumption. If it's minor enough to guess safely, make the call and document the assumption in the README rather than treating either extreme (asking about everything, or asking about nothing) as the default.

The worst outcome is neither asking nor documenting — building on a silent, unstated assumption that the evaluator only discovers when the behavior doesn't match what they expected.

slides.sectionTitle: Skipping tests because "it's just a take-home"
slides.markdown:
"It's just a take-home, not real production code" is a reasonable-sounding thought that leads to a real mistake: the take-home *is* the artifact you're evaluated on, and skipping tests entirely removes a signal evaluators specifically look for. Many rubrics score testing discipline directly, independent of whether the code happens to work.

The distinction to hold onto: you don't need exhaustive coverage (see [take-home-submission-structure](take-home-submission-structure) on prioritizing risky logic), but zero tests on a task with meaningful business logic reads as either an oversight or a belief that testing doesn't matter — neither is the impression you want to leave. Even two or three well-chosen tests on the riskiest path outperforms none.

If you truly ran out of time, say so explicitly rather than letting the absence speak for itself with no context.

slides.sectionTitle: The pairing-round equivalent: silent guessing under time pressure
slides.markdown:
The same instinct that causes silent guessing in a take-home shows up differently, but just as damagingly, in a live pairing round: a candidate under time pressure assumes a requirement rather than asking, because asking feels like it costs precious minutes. In practice, a wrong assumption acted on for ten minutes costs far more than the ten seconds a clarifying question would have taken.

The difference from the take-home version is that a pairing round gives you an interviewer sitting right there — silent guessing here is a strictly worse trade than in an async take-home, since the cost of asking is nearly zero and the interviewer is actively available. Treat any moment of "I think they mean X" as a cue to say it out loud and confirm, not to privately decide and proceed.

This connects directly to time-pressure behavior: rushing under a countdown is exactly when people skip the clarifying question they'd normally ask, so naming the time pressure itself ("I want to make sure I'm not misreading this — does X mean Y?") is often the fix.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a candidate who sends one clarifying email vs one who guesses
slides.markdown:
Two candidates hit the same ambiguous requirement in an async take-home. Their outcomes diverge sharply from a single decision point.

| | Sends one clarifying email | Guesses silently |
|---|---|---|
| Time cost | Minutes, waiting for a reply | None upfront, but risk of hours of rework if wrong |
| Signal sent | Checks assumptions before committing time — a real-ticket instinct | Unknown to the evaluator until the wrong behavior surfaces |
| Worst case | No reply in time — falls back to a documented assumption | Built the wrong thing entirely, discovered at review, unrecoverable before submission |
| Best case | Confirms early, builds correctly with confidence | Guessed right, no visible downside — but this is luck, not skill |

**How to decide:** ask when the ambiguity is genuinely architecture-changing; the downside of one specific, well-timed question is small, and the downside of a wrong silent guess compounds for the rest of the time budget.

slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll know if something's off — I don't need an explicit checklist before I submit."

**Why it's wrong:** every pitfall in this topic is dangerous specifically because it's invisible from the inside while you're mid-task — scope creep feels like productivity, silent guessing feels like decisiveness, skipped tests feel like reasonable time management. A final deliberate check catches what momentum hides.

**Correct model:** before submitting, run through a short checklist explicitly: does everything built trace back to a stated requirement (scope), does the actual time spent match what's disclosed (budget), is every assumption documented rather than silent (ambiguity), and does the riskiest logic have at least one test (coverage). Five minutes running this checklist is cheap insurance against all four pitfalls at once.

slides.sectionTitle: Why these pitfalls are specific to unsupervised formats
slides.markdown:
It's worth being precise about what makes these pitfalls distinct from a live solo whiteboard round's failure modes (getting stuck on an algorithm, mismanaging complexity analysis, freezing under direct observation). Those live pitfalls are caught in real time — an interviewer sees you stuck and the round adjusts. Take-home and pairing pitfalls are dangerous precisely because **no one is there to catch them as they happen**, or in pairing's case, because the pressure of being watched pushes people away from the exact behavior (asking, checking scope) that would prevent them.

This is why the fix for all four pitfalls in this topic is the same underlying habit: build in deliberate checkpoints — a scope check before adding a feature, a time check partway through, a triage step for every ambiguity — rather than trusting that you'll naturally notice drift. Supervision from an interviewer is what these formats remove; deliberate self-checks are how you replace it.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior-level nuance: treating unsupervised work as the actual job simulation
slides.markdown:
A junior candidate treats a take-home or pairing round's unsupervised nature as a loophole — no one's watching, so cut whichever corner is convenient. A senior candidate recognizes it as the opposite: this format is a closer simulation of real, unsupervised engineering work than a live whiteboard round ever was, since most real tickets don't come with someone watching every decision either.

The habits that avoid these four pitfalls — bounding scope explicitly, disclosing actual time spent, triaging ambiguity instead of guessing, testing the risky paths — aren't interview tricks. They're the same habits that make someone trustworthy with an unsupervised real ticket, which is exactly why evaluators weight them so heavily: the format is deliberately testing for the behavior itself, not producing it as an artificial obstacle course.
